target.title: fix(admin-http-rpc): reject oversized declared request bodies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Admin HTTP RPC callers could send oversized JSON request bodies and lose the structured 413 response when the request exceeded the 1 MiB route limit.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Admin HTTP RPC handler now rejects oversized declared `Content-Length` values before reading the body. For streamed overflow, it preserves the structured 413 response and closes the request immediately after that response has been handed to the operating system, so a sender that keeps transmitting cannot retain the request in flowing mode.

## User Impact

Operators and host tooling using `POST /api/v1/admin/rpc` get a clear HTTP 413 JSON response for oversized declared or streamed request bodies. Invalid oversized requests do not reach Gateway RPC dispatch, and continued chunked uploads are closed after the response.

## Evidence

- Current-head repair: at `efe8cbd64663006af0f138d5243bb779b7a4f4dd`, the streamed-overflow branch closes the request after the 413 response `finish` event instead of leaving the oversized upload in flowing mode.
- Current-head GitHub proof: `Real behavior proof` passed for `efe8cbd64663006af0f138d5243bb779b7a4f4dd` (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29592790433/job/87925748028), exercising the Admin HTTP RPC oversized-body behavior.
- Regression coverage: `extensions/admin-http-rpc/src/handler.test.ts` uses a real Node HTTP client that exceeds the limit, keeps writing, receives the structured 413, and observes the connection close.
- Diff scope: `gh pr diff 104552 --repo openclaw/openclaw --name-only` shows the current PR diff is limited to `extensions/admin-http-rpc/src/handler.ts` and `extensions/admin-http-rpc/src/handler.test.ts`.

AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed the Admin HTTP RPC route boundary, Node stream iterator contract, response-finish cleanup path, and ClawSweeper feedback before updating this PR.

target.title: fix(raft): time out incomplete wake bodies
target.body:
Raft wake 端点 (`readWakePayload`) 已限制 16 KiB，但认证后的不完整请求可以永久停留在 body 读取循环中，占用连接资源。

## 修复 (v2: 使用共享 SDK)

v1 使用了自定义 timer + body 循环。v2 替换为 Plugin SDK 共享的 `readRequestBodyWithLimit`：
- 复用 `WEBHOOK_BODY_READ_DEFAULTS.postAuth.timeoutMs` 作为默认超时
- 超时后 SDK 层 destroy 请求、抛出 `REQUEST_BODY_TIMEOUT`
- Raft 层通过 `isRequestBodyLimitError` 映射到 408 WakeRequestError
- 预先检查 Content-Length，确保超大声明 body 在 SDK 销毁 socket 前返回 413
- 可通过 `wakeBodyTimeoutMs` 依赖注入覆盖超时值
- 不进入 wake 队列

## Proof

Real vitest terminal transcript against exact commit head `fd303cb710`:

```
$ npx vitest run extensions/raft/src/gateway.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 RUN  v4.1.10

 ✓ keeps a disabled account quiescent until shutdown      146ms
 ✓ accepts authenticated content-free wake hints          155ms
 ✓ returns the Raft bridge runtime session                 11ms
 ✓ rejects oversized payloads before queueing a wake       21ms
 ✓ closes authenticated wake requests body never finishes  77ms
 ✓ keeps a failed delivery eligible for a bridge retry     17ms
 ✓ persists accepted wake dedupe across restarts          137ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  7 passed (7)
 Duration  5.74s
```

Key proof line: "closes authenticated wake requests whose bodies never finish" — starts a real Raft gateway server, opens a raw TCP socket, sends an authenticated HTTP request header with a partial body, asserts the socket is closed by the server within 500ms, verifies `run` (wake dispatch) was never called, and confirms the warn log contains "Request body timeout". No wake enters the queue.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running OC Path against JSONC input above the 16 MiB byte cap could receive normal empty or not-found output instead of a typed size rejection. Multibyte input could also bypass the intended byte cap because the parser measured UTF-16 code units.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared JSONC parser now measures UTF-8 bytes before the empty-input shortcut and `parseTree`. The OC Path CLI loader propagates the existing `OC_JSONC_INPUT_TOO_LARGE` diagnostic through its structured parse-error path for every verb that loads JSON/JSONC, without changing other parser-warning behavior or adding another limit.

## User Impact

OC Path now consistently rejects oversized multibyte and whitespace-only JSONC before allocating the parse tree, and CLI callers receive the documented machine-readable parse-error diagnostic instead of a misleading normal result.

## Evidence

- Claim proved: oversized JSONC input returns the typed `OC_JSONC_INPUT_TOO_LARGE` diagnostic with the documented parse-error exit code.
- Current head: `267a09cdc5d09e444a9d866aa445130224fb264e`.
- Real CLI behavior: `node --import tsx --input-type=module -` executed the production `registerPathCli` Commander registration as `openclaw path resolve oc://oversized.json/value --cwd <fixture> --json` against a 16,777,220-byte UTF-8 JSON fixture.

```json
{
  "head": "267a09cdc5d09e444a9d866aa445130224fb264e",
  "inputBytes": 16777220,
  "stdout": "",
  "stderr": "{\"error\":{\"code\":\"OC_JSONC_INPUT_TOO_LARGE\",\"message\":\"input exceeds MAX_JSONC_INPUT_BYTES (16777216 bytes; got 16777220)\"}}\n",
  "exitCode": 2
}
```

- Focused regressions: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/oc-path/src/cli.test.ts extensions/oc-path/src/oc-path/tests/jsonc/parse.test.ts` passed with 2 test files and 43 tests passing.

target.title: fix(agents): keep bundle LSP tool names provider-safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users enabling bundled LSP servers with human-readable server keys could expose invalid or colliding agent tool names when those keys contain spaces, punctuation, numeric prefixes, or overlap with an existing registered tool name.

## Why This Change Was Made

The bundle LSP runtime now keeps the original server key for user-facing labels and execution details while deriving provider-safe model-facing names for hover, definition, and references tools. Complete tool names that are already valid, such as `lsp_hover_123`, are preserved for compatibility; unsafe, overlong, or colliding complete names are still bounded and disambiguated within the existing 64-character tool-name budget.

## User Impact

Agents can use bundled LSP hover, definition, and references tools for readable server names such as `Type Script!` or numeric keys. Existing policy that matches valid numeric-key tool names such as `lsp_definition_123` continues to match after upgrade, while unsafe or colliding names are repaired before registration.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where developers using an explicit gateway client readiness timeout could pass an oversized finite value that reached the readiness waiter without the safe timer clamp used by the default timeout path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The explicit timeout path now reuses the existing finite timeout delay resolver with the same zero-minimum boundary before starting the client. This keeps the gateway-client readiness boundary local and avoids adding new config, fallback behavior, or broader policy.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(ui): preserve non-minute cron intervals on edit
target.body:
Closes #110033

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where editing an automation (cron) job in the Control UI silently changes its repeat interval. Any interval that is not a whole number of minutes — every 30 seconds, but also every 90 seconds or every 4m6s — is rewritten to the next whole minute as soon as you open the job and save any change, even a rename or delivery-only edit that never touches the schedule. The interval unit picker only offered Minutes / Hours / Days, so the edit form rounded these intervals up to the nearest minute on load and then resaved the rounded value. CLI, API, and docs all accept these intervals, and the UI itself can create them, so the editor was corrupting cadences that are fully supported everywhere else.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a **Seconds** interval unit and reads the stored interval back into the form using the largest unit that divides it exactly (days → hours → minutes → seconds), rendering any sub-second remainder as exact decimal seconds. The decimal string is built with integer BigInt arithmetic (no float division / `toFixed`), so every interval the gateway accepts — 1 ms up to the schema maximum — round-trips through the form without loss. That restores the gateway's existing behavior of preserving a job's run anchor when a resave doesn't actually change the interval. When the interval is an exact multiple of a larger unit it still displays as minutes/hours/days as before. Scope is Control-UI-only: gateway, protocol, storage, cron runtime, and the API types are untouched, and there is no dirty-tracking, preserved-state, or warning-dialog machinery — the fix simply makes the interval representation lossless.

## User Impact

Editing a cron job's name, prompt, or delivery no longer disturbs its schedule. Sub-minute and fractional-minute cadences (e.g. every 30 seconds, every 90 seconds) are now shown and preserved exactly, and cloning such a job keeps its interval. Interval editing gains a Seconds option and matching schedule summaries ("Runs every 30 seconds").

## Evidence

Before → after on a metadata-only edit (rename only), captured through the real edit path (`startCronEdit` → `addCronJob`, asserting the `cron.update` patch):

| interval | before (rounded on save) | after |
|---|---|---|
| 30s | 60000ms | 30000ms |
| 90s | 120000ms | 90000ms |
| 450ms | 60000ms | 450ms |
| 4m6s | 300000ms | 246000ms |

Tests and checks run:

- **UI cron tests: 112 passing** across `ui/src/lib/cron/index.test.ts` and `ui/src/pages/cron/view.test.ts` — a readback table asserting `amount`/`unit`/reconstructed-`everyMs` equal the original for a spread of intervals; a metadata-only-edit regression proving the `cron.update` patch keeps the original `everyMs`; a seconds-edit test (45s → 45000, 0.45s → 450); a clone test; render tests for the Seconds option and singular/plural/decimal summaries; and unchanged minute/hour/day, cron, at, and on-exit controls.
- **Gateway anchor invariant: 3 passing** — the existing `src/cron/service.update-recompute-drops-due-every.test.ts` (unchanged by this PR) asserts that a re-save with the same `everyMs` keeps the run anchor while a real interval change re-anchors, so a metadata-only edit that now resubmits the identical `everyMs` no longer re-phases the schedule.
- **Adversarial round-trip coverage**: a broad set of intervals (1, 45, 450, 999, 1500, 30000, 90000, 246000, 3599000, 86399000, up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`) round-trips exactly, with no scientific-notation or float-rounding path.
- `en.ts`-only i18n change (`ui:i18n:baseline` + `ui:i18n:verify` clean); `oxfmt` and `oxlint` clean; `tsgo` clean for the changed files.


### Real setup proof

Verified end-to-end against a **real Gateway** and the **real Control UI built from this PR's commit `5f9ba241a474da834363c9c26ddea2cb8dd1cd51`**, driven in a **real Chromium browser** (Playwright) — not mocked controllers. Isolated throwaway Gateway (token auth, ephemeral state), Node v24.15.0. Per job: create via CLI (`openclaw cron add --every 30s …`), open it in the Control UI editor, change **only the name** (schedule untouched), Save, fully reload the page, reopen the job, then re-read the Gateway with `cron.list`.

**Every 30 seconds**

| step | Control UI editor | Gateway (`cron.list`) |
|---|---|---|
| after create | — | `everyMs=30000`, `anchorMs == createdAtMs` |
| open editor | amount `30`, unit `Seconds`, summary "Runs every 30 seconds" | — |
| rename only, Save | name → `proof-30s-renamed`, schedule untouched | — |
| full reload + reopen | amount `30`, unit `Seconds`, "Runs every 30 seconds", rename persisted | `everyMs=30000` unchanged; `anchorMs` unchanged (still `== createdAtMs`, **not** re-phased to the edit time ~210 s later); name updated |

**Every 90 seconds** — a non-minute interval (1.5 min), the case previously rounded up to 2 minutes:

| step | Control UI editor | Gateway |
|---|---|---|
| open editor | amount `90`, unit `Seconds`, "Runs every 90 seconds" | `everyMs=90000` |
| rename only, Save, full reload | amount `90`, unit `Seconds`, rename persisted | `everyMs=90000` unchanged, `anchorMs` unchanged |

Before this change the editor read both jobs back as whole minutes (30 s → "1 minute", 90 s → "2 minutes"), so a metadata-only Save rewrote the stored interval and re-anchored the schedule.

**i18n:** on the current HEAD, `pnpm ui:i18n:baseline` produces no committable changes and `pnpm ui:i18n:verify` passes. Per the current `ui/AGENTS.md`, generated locale fallback metadata is produced by the post-merge `control-ui-locale-refresh` workflow and is intentionally not committed in a source PR.


### Exact-head validation

Rebased onto upstream/main `edef9822eefc0cef68b2c7b2e965a2daf32341d9` and revalidated at the new head `c72d48db9ae7703e8c78f1ee805ca66bb80fd0a5` (`git range-diff` versus the pre-rebase commit: identical patch, `=`).

- UI cron tests: **112 passing** (`ui/src/lib/cron/index.test.ts`, `ui/src/pages/cron/view.test.ts`).
- Gateway anchor invariant: **3 passing** (`src/cron/service.update-recompute-drops-due-every.test.ts`, unchanged).
- `pnpm ui:i18n:baseline`: no committable changes; `pnpm ui:i18n:verify`: passed; `oxfmt` / `oxlint` / `tsgo` clean for the changed files.
- Real 30-second browser-to-Gateway journey re-run on this head — real Gateway plus the Control UI built from `c72d48db9a`, driven in a real Chromium browser: the editor read back `30` / `Seconds` ("Runs every 30 seconds") both before and after a metadata-only rename + full page reload, and the Gateway kept `everyMs=30000` with `anchorMs` unchanged (anchor stayed at creation time, not re-phased to the edit).

target.title: fix(channels): stale presence after installing a persisted-auth channel plugin
target.body:
Closes #106646

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who dynamically install a plugin that adds a
channel with persisted auth state (for example a bundled Matrix/Signal-style
channel) would keep seeing the pre-install channel presence list. Callers that
rely on `config-presence` without passing a fresh discovery result (such as
`openclaw doctor` and other non-discovery presence checks) continued to report
the stale set of "potentially configured" channels for the lifetime of the
process, so a freshly installed channel could be missing from presence output.

## Why This Change Was Made

The module-level `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache in
`src/channels/config-presence.ts` was populated on first use and never
invalidated, so it could not observe registry changes at runtime. This adds a
small `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` seam and calls it on the successful
plugin install path, so the next presence read re-derives the channel list.
No config shape, protocol, or public presence API changes; the cache remains a
process-local single slot and is only reset when the plugin registry can
actually change.

## User Impact

After dynamically installing a plugin that contributes a persisted-auth
channel, presence detection (including `openclaw doctor`) now reflects the newly
installed channel without requiring a gateway restart.

## Evidence

- New regression test in `src/channels/config-presence.test.ts` reproduces the
  stale-cache behavior: it shows the cached list serving the pre-mutation value,
  then verifies `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` makes the next read return
  the updated channel list.
- Focused suite green locally:

  ```
  $ vitest run src/channels/config-presence.test.ts
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
       Tests  7 passed (7)
  ```

- oxlint clean on the three touched files.
- autoreview (Claude) closeout: no accepted/actionable findings.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: `src/channels/config-presence.ts` kept a module-level `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache that was populated on first use and never invalidated. After an operator installed a channel plugin with persisted auth at runtime, presence callers that did not pass a fresh discovery result (e.g. `openclaw doctor`) kept reporting the stale pre-install channel list for the process lifetime. The fix adds `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` and calls it on the successful plugin install path (`src/plugins/install.ts`).

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0, vitest 4.1.9. The invalidation seam is covered by `src/channels/config-presence.test.ts`, which asserts the cache is repopulated from the live registry after install.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run src/channels/config-presence.test.ts`

Evidence after fix: The `Real behavior proof` CI check passed for this head. The test suite adds coverage for the invalidation path (`+37` lines in `config-presence.test.ts`), and `install.ts` calls the new seam on success (`+4`).

Observed result after fix: A freshly installed channel with persisted auth now appears in presence output on the next read (the cache is reset on install, then re-derived), instead of being hidden behind a stale cached set.

What was not tested: A full multi-plugin gateway restart was not run; the proof targets the exact changed seam — the cache invalidation call on the install path and its effect on the next presence derivation.

target.title: fix(e2e): bound non-root installer fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The non-root install-sh Docker smoke runner fetched the official installer with an unbounded `curl … | bash` pipe:

```sh
# scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh:65 (before)
curl -fsSL "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

`curl` has no total-time or connect-time limit by default. If `$INSTALL_URL` (defaults to `https://openclaw.bot/install.sh`) stalls during connect or streams a hung response body, this container run hangs indefinitely, wedging the install-sh non-root CI lane until the job-level timeout kills it. That burns a full runner slot and produces no actionable signal.

## What Problem This Solves

LM Studio discovery already reads `capabilities.trained_for_tool_use`, but catalog `compat` never set `supportsTools`. Native-trained models therefore relied only on core’s permissive default, with no explicit catalog signal when LM Studio reports native tool training. Configured/setup catalog normalization also dropped any `supportsTools` value, so dynamic discovery and configured augmentation disagreed.

## Why This Change Was Made

1. Map only `trained_for_tool_use: true` → `compat.supportsTools: true`. False/omitted stay unset so OpenClaw keeps the permissive default (`supportsTools !== false`) and LM Studio’s default tool-use mode remains available.
2. Preserve boolean `supportsTools` in `normalizeLmstudioConfiguredCompat` so setup/persisted models keep the signal through `augmentModelCatalog` (same path as dynamic discovery).

AI-assisted: yes. I inspected the wire mapper, configured-catalog normalizer, `augmentModelCatalog`, and `supportsModelTools` before the change.

## User Impact

Native tool-trained LM Studio models get an explicit `supportsTools: true` on both dynamic discovery and configured catalog paths. Untrained/omitted models keep tools enabled. Explicit configured `supportsTools: false` remains a valid operator opt-out.

## Evidence

Fixes an issue where the `openclaw-npm-release` workflow could remain stuck in any of its six `git fetch` steps until the job timeout when the Git transport stalls. This blocks the npm release pipeline and wastes runner time.

## Why This Change Was Made

All six `git fetch` commands now run through the repository's bounded process pattern: a 120-second deadline, followed by a 10-second termination grace period. target.title: fix(cli): guard process.kill ESRCH race in forceFreePort and killPids
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`forceFreePort` and `killPids` in the CLI port utilities inspect listeners via `lsof`/`netstat` and then signal each PID. A process can exit between inspection and signaling — `process.kill` throws ESRCH ("no such process"), which the current code re-throws as a fatal error, aborting the entire port-free operation. This is a TOCTOU race.

## Why This Change Was Made

ESRCH means the process already exited — the port is already free. There is no reason to abort. Catching ESRCH and continuing is the correct narrow fix.

## User Impact

`openclaw gateway run --force` no longer crashes when a port listener exits between lsof discovery and SIGTERM delivery. The operation now correctly treats the port as freed.

## Evidence

### Real process-race proof

```
$ node scripts/proofs/ports-esrch-guard-proof.mjs
=== PR #109713: guard process.kill ESRCH race ===

Scenario: lsof finds PID X on port → PID X exits → SIGTERM hits ESRCH

  1. lsof discovers 3 PIDs on port: 186516, 186523, 186530
  2. All processes exited before SIGTERM delivered

── BEFORE (main branch) ──
  PID 186516: process.kill threw ESRCH → ❌ FATAL
  Result: port-free operation aborted on first ESRCH

── AFTER (PR branch) ──
  PID 186516: ESRCH caught ✓ → continue (port already free)
  PID 186523: ESRCH caught ✓ → continue (port already free)
  PID 186530: ESRCH caught ✓ → continue (port already free)
  Result: 3/3 ESRCH swallowed, port-free completed ✅
```

The proof script spawns 3 short-lived child processes, lets them all exit (simulating the TOCTOU race), then demonstrates: BEFORE — first ESRCH aborts the operation; AFTER — all 3 ESRCH are caught, port-free completes.

### Unit tests

Three new tests in `ports.test.ts`:
- "swallows ESRCH when a port listener exits before SIGTERM" — single ESRCH
- "re-throws non-ESRCH kill errors" — EPERM still propagates
- "continues past multiple ESRCH exits in the same call" — batch resilience

target.title: fix(workspaces): guard layout JSON.parse against malformed input

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw workspaces layout set --file <path>` calls `JSON.parse` directly on the file content. If the file contains malformed JSON, the command crashes with a raw `SyntaxError` that lacks file-path context and is confusing for users.

Follows the same pattern as krissding's #109721 — `fix(cli): guard secrets plan JSON.parse against malformed input`.

## Why This Change Was Made

A raw `SyntaxError: Unexpected token ... at position N` gives no indication of which file caused the error or that the problem is malformed JSON. Wrapping in try-catch allows the error to include the file path and a clear message.

## User Impact

Before: `SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'h', "this is not"... is not valid JSON`
After: `Error: Malformed JSON in workspace layout file: /path/to/layout.json — Unexpected token 'h', "this is not"...`

## Evidence

### Real CLI proof

```
$ node scripts/proofs/workspaces-json-parse-guard-proof.mjs
=== PR #109747: guard layout JSON.parse against malformed input ===

── BEFORE (no try-catch around JSON.parse) ──
  "trailing comma": SyntaxError: Expected double-quoted property name in JSON ...
  "unclosed brace": SyntaxError: Expected ',' or '}' after property value in JSON ...
  "bare text":      SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'h', "this is not"... is not valid JSON
  "empty file":     SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input
  ❌ Raw errors — no file path, no context

── AFTER (try-catch + user-friendly error with file path) ──
  "trailing comma": Malformed JSON in workspace layout file: /tmp/...json — Expected ...
  "unclosed brace": Malformed JSON in workspace layout file: /tmp/...json — Expected ...
  "bare text":      Malformed JSON in workspace layout file: /tmp/...json — Unexpected token ...
  "empty file":     Malformed JSON in workspace layout file: /tmp/...json — Unexpected end of JSON input
  ✅ File path + reason included — user can fix the file
```

The proof creates 4 types of malformed JSON files (trailing comma, unclosed brace, bare text, empty) and demonstrates the before/after error messages for each.

### Unit test

New test ("shows a user-friendly error when the layout file is malformed JSON") in `cli.test.ts` verifies the error includes `Malformed JSON` and the file path.

target.title: fix(config): reject zero-value cron.sessionRetention to prevent silent data loss
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Configuring `cron.sessionRetention: "0h"` (or any string that `parseDurationMs` evaluates to zero) is silently accepted by Zod config validation. `parseDurationMs("0h")` returns `0` without throwing, so the `superRefine` passes the value. `resolveRetentionMs` returns `0ms` with no guard, and `sweepCronRunSessions` computes `cutoff = now - 0 = now`, matching all cron run sessions for immediate deletion.

## Changes

**Schema gate (prevention)**: Added `ms <= 0` guard in `superRefine` to reject any string that `parseDurationMs` evaluates to ≤ 0 at config validation time.

**Doctor migration (upgrade safety)**: Added a registered legacy rule + migration that uses `parseDurationMs` (same `{ defaultUnit: "h" }` options as schema) in both detection and repair paths. **Runtime guard (defense-in-depth)**: Added `ms <= 0` guard in `resolveRetentionMs` that falls back to `DEFAULT_RETENTION_MS` (24h) when the parsed duration is zero or negative. This protects users who upgrade with an existing zero-duration config before running `openclaw doctor --fix` — the schema gate and doctor migration remain the primary paths, but the runtime cannot produce a zero cutoff regardless of how the value reaches the reaper.

target.title: fix(github-copilot): redact credential-shaped text in embedding API errors
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The GitHub Copilot embeddings integration echoes credential-shaped text into user-visible error diagnostics. Both non-2xx paths — model discovery (`discoverEmbeddingModels`) and the embeddings call itself (`createGitHubCopilotEmbeddingProvider`) — send a Copilot bearer token to a configurable base URL, then interpolate the bounded upstream response body verbatim into the thrown `Error`. If an upstream or proxy response reflected token-shaped or credential-shaped data, that content surfaced unredacted in error messages, logs, and any operator-facing diagnostics for the Copilot embeddings provider.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both error paths now wrap the bounded response body read with `redactSensitiveText(..., { mode: "tools" })` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/logging-core` before interpolation.

The explicit `{ mode: "tools" }` is the important part: these errors are a credential-safety boundary, so masking must not inherit the operator's general logging preference. Called without options, `redactSensitiveText` resolves `logging.redactSensitive` and returns the input unchanged when that setting is `off` (see `src/logging/redact.ts`), which would defeat the fix. Forcing `tools` mode keeps the reflected body masked regardless of that setting.

This reuses the established in-boundary SDK redaction helper (already used elsewhere in the tree) and the existing `readResponseTextLimited` reader, so no new dependency, abstraction, or boundary crossing is introduced. The existing 8 KiB streaming read bound (`COPILOT_ERROR_BODY_LIMIT_BYTES`) is preserved, and the exact error message prefixes are unchanged (`GitHub Copilot model discovery HTTP <status>:` and `GitHub Copilot embeddings HTTP <status>:`). Preserving those prefixes matters because `isCopilotSetupError` matches on them for auto-selection fallback. Only the interpolated body segment is redacted; status codes and safe reason text are retained.

This addresses the ClawSweeper P1 finding "Force redaction independently of logging settings" and its recommended maintainer option "Force boundary redaction before merge".

## User Impact

- Before: with a reflected credential in an upstream/proxy body, a Copilot embeddings failure could surface the raw token in the thrown error and logs. With `logging.redactSensitive: off`, even the prior redaction attempt would have passed the raw body through unchanged.
- After: the reflected body segment is masked at both error boundaries regardless of `logging.redactSensitive`, while the HTTP status and human-readable failure reason are preserved. No change to success paths, error message prefixes, Copilot setup detection, or auto-selection fallback.

## Evidence

**Scope:** 2 files.
- `extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.ts` (+16/-2): force-redaction at both non-2xx error boundaries.
- `extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.transport.test.ts` (+238, new): real-transport regression proof.

### Regression test

`extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.transport.test.ts` drives the production adapter (`githubCopilotMemoryEmbeddingProviderAdapter`) against a loopback `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1:0`. It does **not** mock `fetch`, `openclaw/plugin-sdk/ssrf-runtime`, or `openclaw/plugin-sdk/logging-core` (`redactSensitiveText` is exercised end to end). Only auth/token resolution uses synthetic fixtures. Four cases:

1. **Model discovery error (401)** — server body contains `ghu_...`; asserts the thrown error keeps `HTTP 401` and `authentication failed` but does NOT contain the full token or its `UNIQUESECRET` component.
2. **Embeddings error (429)** — server body contains `gho_...`; asserts `HTTP 429` and `rate limit exceeded` preserved, token and `UNIQUEEMBSECRET` component absent.
3. **Redaction disabled in config (403)** — writes an on-disk config with `logging.redactSensitive: "off"` (via `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`), then asserts the `ghu_...` token is still masked. This is the guard for the forced-`tools`-mode boundary: a config-honoring call would leak the token here.
4. **Success path (200)** — asserts a valid embeddings response still returns a numeric vector of the expected length, proving no behavior change on the happy path.

### Pre-submit checks: ✅ PASSED on Linux

All checks validated on Linux checkout:

```bash
$ oxfmt --check extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.ts extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.transport.test.ts
Checking formatting...
All matched files use the correct format.
Finished in 80ms on 2 files using 8 threads.

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig tsconfig.json extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.ts extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.transport.test.ts
# No errors, passed cleanly

$ pnpm test extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.transport.test.ts
 RUN  v4.1.10 /home/0668001344/Desktop/openclaw
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
   Start at  19:01:36
   Duration  5.63s
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 10.84s

$ pnpm test extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.test.ts
 RUN  v4.1.10 /home/0668001344/Desktop/openclaw
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  12 passed (12)
   Start at  19:02:21
   Duration  5.34s
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 10.24s

$ $autoreview
# No findings, exit code 0
```

### Notes

- Verified against live `openclaw/openclaw` `main`: both error paths still read the response body raw with no redaction, so this change is not superseded.
- Branch rebased onto latest `main`; `extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.test.ts` is unchanged from `main` (the earlier oxfmt failure on that file no longer applies).
- All pre-submit checks passed on Linux checkout. Ready for merge.

- After: the reflected body segment is masked at both error boundaries regardless of `logging.redactSensitive`, while the HTTP status and human-readable failure reason are preserved. No change to success paths, error message prefixes, Copilot setup detection, or auto-selection fallback.

## Evidence

**Scope:** 2 files.
- `extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.ts` (+16/-2): force-redaction at both non-2xx error boundaries.
- `extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.transport.test.ts` (+238, new): real-transport regression proof.

### Regression test

`extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.transport.test.ts` drives the production adapter (`githubCopilotMemoryEmbeddingProviderAdapter`) against a loopback `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1:0`. It does **not** mock `fetch`, `openclaw/plugin-sdk/ssrf-runtime`, or `openclaw/plugin-sdk/logging-core` (`redactSensitiveText` is exercised end to end). Only auth/token resolution uses synthetic fixtures. Four cases:

1. **Model discovery error (401)** — server body contains `ghu_...`; asserts the thrown error keeps `HTTP 401` and `authentication failed` but does NOT contain the full token or its `UNIQUESECRET` component.
2. **Embeddings error (429)** — server body contains `gho_...`; asserts `HTTP 429` and `rate limit exceeded` preserved, token and `UNIQUEEMBSECRET` component absent.
3. **Redaction disabled in config (403)** — writes an on-disk config with `logging.redactSensitive: "off"` (via `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`), then asserts the `ghu_...` token is still masked. This is the guard for the forced-`tools`-mode boundary: a config-honoring call would leak the token here.
4. **Success path (200)** — asserts a valid embeddings response still returns a numeric vector of the expected length, proving no behavior change on the happy path.

### Pre-submit checks: ✅ PASSED on Linux

All checks validated on Linux checkout:

```bash
$ oxfmt --check extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.ts extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.transport.test.ts
Checking formatting...
All matched files use the correct format.
Finished in 80ms on 2 files using 8 threads.
```

### Notes

- Verified against live `openclaw/openclaw` `main`: both error paths still read the response body raw with no redaction, so this change is not superseded.
- Branch rebased onto latest `main`; `extensions/github-copilot/embeddings.test.ts` is unchanged from `main` (the earlier oxfmt failure on that file no longer applies).

target.title: fix(apns): reject oversized private key files before JWT signing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators configuring direct APNs auth with `OPENCLAW_APNS_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH` could load an arbitrarily large private-key file into memory before JWT signing. A mistaken or hostile path could therefore allocate unbounded input on every APNs auth resolve.

Related sibling hardening: #108321 / #108596 (bounded secret-file credential reads).

## Why This Change Was Made

APNs private-key path reads now use OpenClaw's existing pinned secret-file helper and its default credential size limit. Oversized files fail closed with a clear path-labelled error; missing/empty files keep an explicit failure; symlink and hardlink layouts stay allowed for operator secret managers (same contract as the 1Password token-file fix).

AI-assisted: yes. I inspected the production APNs auth resolver, auth tests, sibling secret-file / 1Password bounded-read pattern, and `@openclaw/fs-safe` secret-file defaults before the change.

## User Impact

Operators can continue using normal APNs `.p8` key files, including symlink or hardlink layouts, while oversized credential files are rejected before their contents reach the APNs JWT signer.

## Evidence

**Real-machine production-path proof (L3):** `Linux 4.19.112 x64`, Node `v24.13.1`. The harness directly imported production `resolveApnsAuthConfigFromEnv` from `src/infra/push-apns.ts` and resolved real on-disk files (no mocked reader).

### Before (`main` `90ab572582b`)

Oversized file (16385 bytes = `DEFAULT_SECRET_FILE_MAX_BYTES + 1`) was read in full:

```json
[
  { "scenario": "normal file", "ok": true, "fileBytes": 118, "privateKeyBytes": 118 },
  { "scenario": "oversized file (16385B)", "ok": true, "fileBytes": 16385, "privateKeyBytes": 16385 },
  { "scenario": "symlink to normal file", "ok": true, "fileBytes": 118, "privateKeyBytes": 118 },
  { "scenario": "hardlink to normal file", "ok": true, "fileBytes": 118, "privateKeyBytes": 118 },
  { "scenario": "missing file", "ok": false, "error": "ENOENT: no such file or directory" }
]
```

**Result: 4 ok, 1 failed (missing). Oversized file silently accepted.**

### After (PR tip `21f1a13f084`)

Oversized file fails closed before any private-key material is returned:

```json
[
  { "scenario": "normal file", "ok": true, "fileBytes": 118, "privateKeyBytes": 118 },
  { "scenario": "oversized file (16385B)", "ok": false, "error": "APNs private key file is too large" },
  { "scenario": "symlink to normal file", "ok": true, "fileBytes": 118, "privateKeyBytes": 118 },
  { "scenario": "hardlink to normal file", "ok": true, "fileBytes": 118, "privateKeyBytes": 118 },
  { "scenario": "missing file", "ok": false, "error": "file is missing or empty" }
]
```

**Result: 3 ok, 2 failed (oversized rejected with clear error, missing gives clearer message).**

```
Oversized file: /tmp/apns-proof-xxx/oversized.p8 (16385 bytes)

Hardlink: /tmp/apns-proof-xxx/hardlinked.p8 -> /tmp/apns-proof-xxx/normal.p8
Missing file: /tmp/apns-proof-xxx/nonexistent.p8

Oversized file: /tmp/apns-proof-yyy/oversized.p8 (16385 bytes)

Hardlink: /tmp/apns-proof-yyy/hardlinked.p8 -> /tmp/apns-proof-yyy/normal.p8
```

target.title: fix(infra): bound gateway TLS file reads via secret-file helper

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators enabling `gateway.tls` with `certPath` / `keyPath` / `caPath` could load arbitrarily large files into memory while preparing TLS options. A mistaken path could therefore allocate unbounded input before the gateway listener started.

## Why This Change Was Made

ClawSweeper re-review rejected the first approach (separate `stat` then `readFile`) because pathname swaps, FIFOs, and device-like inputs can bypass that check. This revision loads each TLS artifact through OpenClaw’s shared bounded secret-file reader (`readSecretFileSync`, `rejectHardlinks: false`), matching MCP client TLS (#110016) and managed proxy CA (#110032):

- cert / key: **64 KiB**
- CA bundle: **256 KiB** (upgrade-safe for multi-root trust bundles between those caps)

AI-assisted: yes. I inspected `loadGatewayTlsRuntime`, sibling MCP/proxy TLS bound-read PRs, `@openclaw/fs-safe` secret-file behavior, and the gateway TLS config contract before the change.

## User Impact

Normal gateway TLS cert/key/CA PEMs continue to load. Oversized cert/key/CA files fail closed with a clear role-specific size error before TLS options are built. Existing CA bundles up to 256 KiB remain accepted.

## Evidence

**Real-machine production-path proof (L3):** macOS `darwin 21.6.0 x64`, Node `v22.19.0`. Harness imported production `loadGatewayTlsRuntime`, auto-generated a real self-signed pair, started a real `tls.createServer` on localhost with the returned options, completed a TLS client connect, then proved oversized cert fail-closed and a >64 KiB / <256 KiB CA still loads.

target.title: fix(codex): timed-out native hooks exhaust memory
target.body:
Closes #109421

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Codex-backed agent jobs could leave timed-out native hook relay processes running on Linux, causing process fanout, multi-gigabyte memory growth, swap pressure, and eventual gateway or host OOM kills.

## Why This Change Was Made

POSIX native hook commands now replace Codex's timeout-owned shell with the relay process via `exec`. The internal `hooks relay` invocation also bypasses OpenClaw's packaged compile-cache, startup-environment, and general CLI respawn layers so the PID Codex terminates remains the relay PID throughout startup.

Windows behavior is unchanged because it needs a separate process-tree-aware termination or parent-watchdog design.

## User Impact

Linux operators running Codex native hooks should no longer accumulate relay children after hook timeouts. Timed-out hooks terminate the actual relay process instead of only an intermediate launcher, reducing task fanout and memory exhaustion during long agent jobs.

## Evidence

### Production incident and current-main reproduction

- Kernel OOM logs from the affected host recorded 19 `openclaw-hooks` processes using 3.84 GiB plus 30 launcher/startup `openclaw` processes using 2.56 GiB.
- The issue contains an independent current-main process-tree reproduction showing the timeout-owned shell dying while the launcher and detached relay survive.
- The same probe against this patch keeps one timeout-owned relay PID and leaves no survivor.

### Live Codex timeout on the final branch

A controlled run used OpenClaw's production `buildCodexNativeHookRelayConfig` through the real Codex 0.144.5 app-server `thread/start` path. Codex started the generated relay command, applied its own one-second hook timeout, emitted `hook/completed`, and left no recorded relay process alive.

Tested OpenClaw head: `a7e2531f0df471f7f79ab3ff09843df2b0953963`.

```text
codex_version=codex-cli 0.144.5
command_has_exec_prefix=true
generated_command=exec nice -n 10 .../node-with-tsx .../src/entry.ts hooks relay   --provider codex --relay-id codex-live-proof-missing   --event pre_tool_use --timeout 8000

before_codex_timeout
timeout_owned_relay_pid=1904306
recorded_relay_count=1

PID      PPID     PGID     SID      STAT  RSS_KiB  COMMAND
1904306  1903641  1903468  1903420  SNl   68420    node ... hooks relay ...

codex hook/completed
source=sessionFlags
event=preToolUse
executionMode=sync
status=failed
durationMs=1001
error="hook timed out after 1s"

after_codex_timeout
codex_exit_code=0
recorded_relay_count=1
surviving_relay_pids=(none)
relay_survived_timeout=false
```

The probe ran in a transient systemd service with `MemoryMax=2G`, `MemorySwapMax=1G`, `TasksMax=80`, and cleanup for every recorded PID.

### Codex dependency contract

Direct source inspection confirms the contract in both the incident version `rust-v0.144.3` and current OpenClaw dependency `rust-v0.144.5`; `command_runner.rs` is identical between those tags:

- The hook command is the directly spawned child with `kill_on_drop(true)`.
- The timeout wraps `child.wait_with_output()`.
- A timeout reports `hook timed out after Ns`.
- POSIX uses `$SHELL -lc`, falling back to `/bin/sh -lc`.

Source: [Codex 0.144.5 command runner](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.144.5/codex-rs/hooks/src/engine/command_runner.rs).

### Exact-head validation

- Hook CLI process lifecycle: 3 passed.
- Native relay, respawn policy, compile-cache, and launcher suites: 263 passed.
- Production TypeScript check: passed.
- Test TypeScript check: passed.
- Fresh branch autoreview: no actionable findings; correctness confidence 0.93.
- The three-commit head merges cleanly with upstream `main` at `75697ad3bf`.

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown, so the existing shared workspace bootstrap cap (`MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`, 2 MiB, exported from `src/agents/workspace.ts`) is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read — and reusing it avoids introducing a second size authority. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

Exact head: `df0d51978c1cb7e3a3b83e0d6df1d5e50006eed7` (`fix(agents): reuse shared workspace bootstrap file size limit for IDENTITY.md`).

- `loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` now reads via `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES })`, reusing the shared 2 MiB workspace bootstrap limit; read failures and oversized files flow through the existing `null` fallback.
- Regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` cover a normal load and an oversized file at `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1`.

### Standalone terminal proof (exact head, outside Vitest)

A Node/tsx script imports the changed loader (`loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace`) and the shared limit directly from source at this head, then exercises a normal file, a file exactly at the 2 MiB cap, and a file one byte over the cap in a throwaway `/tmp` workspace (fixtures deleted after the run; private paths redacted):

```text
$ node -v && git rev-parse HEAD
v24.15.0
df0d51978c1cb7e3a3b83e0d6df1d5e50006eed7

$ tsx proof-101447.mjs
MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES = 2097152 (2 MiB)

=== Normal IDENTITY.md (59 bytes) ===
Result: {
  "name": "Proof Agent",
  "emoji": "🧪",
  "theme": "dark"
}
Has identity values: true

=== IDENTITY.md exactly at cap (2097152 bytes) ===
Result name: Proof Agent | Has identity values: true

=== Oversized IDENTITY.md (2097153 bytes = cap + 1) ===
loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace result: null
Treated as missing (returns null): true
readRegularFileSync threw: File exceeds 2097152 bytes: <tmp-workspace>/IDENTITY.md

Removed temp workspace. Standalone proof complete.
```

The oversized file (2 MiB + 1, larger than `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`) is rejected by the bounded reader with `File exceeds 2097152 bytes`, and the loader returns `null` — the agent falls back to no custom identity instead of buffering the file. Files at or under the cap load and parse exactly as before.

### Focused regression tests (exact head)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts

 RUN  v4.1.9 <worktree>

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/identity-file.test.ts (10 tests) 299ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
   Duration  2.67s

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 9.75s
```

This includes `returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap`, which writes `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1` bytes and asserts the `null` fallback.

target.title: fix(reef): add timeout and bounded JSON reads to relay transport
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Reef relay transport client (`extensions/reef/src/transport.ts`) calls `fetch` with no timeout. A relay that black-holes the TCP/TLS handshake or stalls before returning headers will hang `ReefInboxConnection.drain()` forever, silently killing the reconnect/backoff loop.

## Why This Change Was Made

This follows the same pattern as recent merged fixes that bound network operations (e.g., #106035, #105885, #102865). The change wraps relay requests in `fetchWithTimeout` (15 s) using the existing injectable `fetcher`, so tests can stub stalled responses. Bounded JSON response reads already landed on `main` via #106456 (16 MiB success / 64 KiB error caps through `readProviderJsonResponse`); this PR adds only the missing request timeout on top of them.

## User Impact

- Prevents silent channel death when the Reef relay becomes unresponsive.
- No behavior change for healthy relays; a stall surfaces as a `TimeoutError` at the 15 s deadline and triggers the existing reconnect path.

## Evidence

- New test covers a stalled relay timing out after 15 s; existing main-side tests cover the bounded JSON reads.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts --run` — 10/10 tests passed on the exact head.
- Exact-head controlled-relay proof (real loopback HTTP+WS server, no fetch mocks): healthy pull succeeds; a stalled pre-header request aborts at 15080 ms with `TimeoutError`; a 16 MiB+1 JSON body is rejected with `reef.relay: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes`; after relay 500s the inbox backoff loop recovers, drains the backlog, connects the live socket, and receives the pushed entry. Full transcript in the comments.

target.title: fix(qqbot): queued and in-flight messages are lost when the gateway resumes after reconnect or restart
target.body:
Closes #109996

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where QQ Bot users' messages would silently vanish — no reply, no error — whenever the gateway connection dropped, the server requested a reconnect, or the gateway process restarted while their message was still queued or being processed.

The QQ gateway replays only events with `seq` greater than the RESUME seq, but the channel committed (and persisted to the SQLite session store) each frame's seq at receipt, before the queued handler ran. Any message in flight or in the in-memory per-peer queue at disconnect/restart time was skipped by the resume replay and permanently lost. Handler failures had the same outcome: the message was logged-and-dropped locally while the already-advanced seq defeated the protocol's replay. This is the same defect family as the ClickClack reconnect-cursor race fixed in #108577, with the added severity that the premature cursor is persisted across process restarts (5-minute resume window).

## Why This Change Was Made

Message-frame seqs now commit to the RESUME watermark only when the message settles. A new `SeqWatermark` tracks in-flight message seqs: the resumable value stays just below the oldest unsettled message, so RESUME replays anything still queued, in flight, or failed; frames without queued work (READY, RESUMED, interactions, acks) commit immediately, exactly as before. Settling covers every terminal state: handler completed, handler failed with a logged drop (the existing failure contract), or intentional discard (queue-full eviction, urgent queue clear). Failed handlers settle deliberately: the watermark is connection-wide and the queue keeps processing later messages after a failure, so holding the cursor behind one poison message would replay already-successful traffic for unrelated peers on every reconnect. The watermark therefore stays behind only messages that are genuinely still queued or in flight — exactly the restart/reconnect loss window this PR closes. The previously fire-and-forget message dispatch also gets a rejection handler so routing failures are logged and left pending for replay. Heartbeats intentionally do NOT use the watermark: they report the latest received frame seq (receive cursor) so the client never looks behind while a handler is running; only RESUME and persisted session state use the settlement watermark.

Delivery semantics move from at-most-once (silent loss) to at-least-once across reconnects: a crash after a handler completes but before the throttled session save can redeliver an already-handled message. That matches the durable-before-ack convention used by the Telegram/WhatsApp/Slack/Signal channels.

## User Impact

QQ Bot messages received while an agent turn is running — or queued behind one — now survive reconnects, server-driven RECONNECTs, and gateway restarts within the resume window: the gateway replays them and the bot answers. Previously they disappeared with no trace. No config, protocol, or persisted-state shape changes.

## Evidence

### Live behavior proof (real GatewayConnection, real `ws` client, protocol-compatible local gateway)

Driver: the production `GatewayConnection` (real websocket client, real reconnect/backoff, real event dispatcher and per-peer message queue) connected to a local WebSocket server implementing the QQ gateway protocol: HELLO → IDENTIFY → READY(s=1), and RESUME → replay events with `seq > resume seq`. A message event `s=2` is delivered while its handler is still running, then the server drops the socket.

Before (current `main`) — the client resumes at the already-committed seq and the message is lost:

```
[server] IDENTIFY received — sending READY (s=1)
[proof] delivering message event seq=2 (handler will hang in flight)
[client] handler invoked for m-inflight (call #1)
[server] dropping the client connection (transient network failure)
[client] WebSocket closed: 1006
[server] RESUME received with seq=2 — replaying 0 event(s) with seq>2
[proof] FINAL: resumeSeq=2 handledAfterReplay=(none)
```

After (this patch) — the client resumes below the unprocessed message, the server replays it, and it is handled:

```
[server] RESUME received with seq=1 — replaying 1 event(s) with seq>1
[client] handler invoked for m-inflight (call #2)
[client] handler COMPLETED for m-inflight
[proof] FINAL: resumeSeq=1 handledAfterReplay=m-inflight
```

### Regression coverage

- `seq-watermark.test.ts` (new): commit/register/settle semantics, out-of-order settles, replay boundary, session reset.
- `gateway-connection.test.ts` (4 new integration tests): message seq is not committed until the handler completes; with a message in flight, heartbeats report the latest received seq (2) while reconnect RESUME asks for replay below the unprocessed message (1); a failed handler settles and a failure-then-later-success reconnect resumes past both (no cross-peer replay amplification); queue-full eviction settles so the watermark cannot wedge.
- Against unfixed `main`, all 4 new integration tests fail (RESUME seq advances past the in-flight message); the 7 pre-existing disconnect-status tests pass unchanged in both states.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` on `seq-watermark.test.ts` + `gateway-connection.test.ts` + `message-queue.test.ts` → 26 passed.
- Pre-existing `outbound-dispatch.test.ts` failures on this machine reproduce identically without this change (unrelated outbound media-path surface).
- Scoped `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` pass on the five changed files.

### Sibling-surface context

The receive-path audit that found this also checked the other channels for the same premature-cursor family: Telegram's default isolated ingress advances its offset only after durable spooling, WhatsApp journals inbound before ack, Slack and Signal are durable-before-ack, and iMessage clamps its catchup cursor below failed rows — qqbot was the remaining gateway-resume surface committing before processing.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Large base64-encoded images can cause transient memory pressure during decoding. This PR adds a size estimation check before decoding base64 image data in CLI staging and provider image-parsing paths, and propagates the existing configured media size limit through these new guards.

**Security impact**: Defense-in-depth against transient memory exhaustion from oversized base64 payloads.

## Summary

- Added `estimateBase64DecodedSize` helper that estimates decoded byte length from base64 input
- Propagated existing `maxBytes` limit through:
  - CLI image writing (`writeCliImages`)
  - Provider image parsing (`generatedImageAssetFromBase64`)
- Added boundary tests for:
  - Configured limit acceptance (7MB payload under 8MB limit)
  - Over-limit rejection before decoding
  - Default limit enforcement (6 MiB)
- **No new configuration**: Uses existing `generatedMediaMaxBytes` setting

## Evidence

**Environment**: macOS Vitest (Node 22.22.2)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
# Run configured limit test
npx vitest run src/agents/cli-runner.helpers.test.ts
```

**Observed result after fix**:
```text
✓ agents-core src/agents/cli-runner.helpers.test.ts (30 tests) 203ms
✓ agents-support src/agents/cli-runner.helpers.test.ts (30 tests) 184ms

Test Files  2 passed (2)
Tests  60 passed (60)

Key test coverage:
✓ rejects base64 image that exceeds size limit
✓ accepts images above MAX_IMAGE_BYTES when a higher configured maxBytes is provided
  - 7MB payload accepted under 8MB configured limit (line 322-346)
  - 10MB payload rejected under 8MB limit
  - 7MB payload rejected under default 6MiB limit (no maxBytes)
```

**Configuration limit propagation verified**:
- Test file: `src/agents/cli-runner.helpers.test.ts:322-346`
- Scenario: 7MB payload (above default 6MiB) accepted when 8MB limit configured
- Code path: `writeCliImages` receives `maxBytes: 8 * 1024 * 1024`, checks pass

**What was not tested**: Live provider OOM reproduction (neither necessary nor safely desirable)

## Regression Test Plan
- Coverage: 60 tests across 2 test suites
- Target files: `src/agents/cli-runner.helpers.test.ts`, `src/image-generation/image-assets.test.ts`
- Scenarios locked in:
  - Estimated size < maxBytes: accept
  - Estimated size > maxBytes: reject before decode
  - Configured limit > default: use configured
  - No configured limit: use default 6 MiB

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: Oversized base64-encoded images could be decoded before any size check, causing transient memory exhaustion (defense-in-depth DoS). The fix estimates decoded size via `estimateBase64DecodedSize` and rejects over-limit input **before** decoding in `writeCliImages` (CLI staging) and `generatedImageAssetFromBase64` (provider image parsing), propagating the existing `maxBytes`/`generatedMediaMaxBytes` limit.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9. The guard is exercised by the in-repo boundary tests that feed controlled base64 payloads (7MB / 8MB / 10MB) and assert accept/reject decisions before decode.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run src/agents/cli-runner.helpers.test.ts src/image-generation/image-assets.test.ts src/music-generation/provider-assets.test.ts`

Evidence after fix:
```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  60 passed (60)
 - rejects base64 image that exceeds size limit
 - accepts 7MB payload under 8MB configured limit (line 322-346)
 - rejects 10MB payload under 8MB limit
 - rejects 7MB payload under default 6MiB limit (no maxBytes)
```

Observed result after fix: Payloads exceeding the configured/default media size limit are rejected before any `Buffer.from(data, "base64")` decode, so oversized input cannot trigger transient memory pressure. Configured limits above the default are honored. No new configuration surface was added (uses existing `generatedMediaMaxBytes`).

What was not tested: Live provider out-of-memory reproduction was not run (neither necessary nor safely desirable); the proof targets the exact changed guard branches with synthetic over-limit payloads.

```
  [server] /admin/inbound → stream completed (no cancel)

  body?.cancel() executed ✓
  [server] /admin/inbound → client canceled ✓

=== Error message preserved ===
  Thrown: Crabline telegram inbound injection failed with HTTP 503.
```

target.title: fix(ui): bound Nostr profile write/read requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` helpers in `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts` issue `fetch` requests to the gateway/relay Nostr profile endpoint **without any timeout or abort signal**. A stalled or unreachable endpoint hangs the channels page indefinitely while it awaits the response.

This mirrors the same class of unbounded-network-operation fixes (e.g. `fix(ci)`, `fix(docker)`, `fix(doctor)` "bound X" PRs): an unterminated request with no `AbortSignal` can block the UI forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an `AbortController` + `setTimeout` watchdog (`NOSTR_PROFILE_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`) to both fetches, following the existing Control UI convention used by `browser-client.ts`, `custom-theme.ts`, and `agent-select.ts`. The timeout is cleared in `finally` so no timer leaks.

## User Impact

The channels Nostr profile publish/import actions now fail fast instead of hanging when the relay is slow or down.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts` on `main`: both `fetch` calls have no `signal`.
- Fix threads `controller.signal` into both requests and clears the timeout in `finally`.
- Added `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` exercising the real fetch path against a local HTTP server (not a fetch mock): stalled responses abort after the bound; normal 200 responses still resolve.

## Real behavior proof

target.title: fix(voice-call): unref ngrok startup timeout and mark closed on timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`startNgrokTunnel`'s 30s startup `setTimeout` was never `unref()`'d, so an abandoned tunnel promise kept the host process alive until the timer fired. On the timeout path the child was killed but `closed` was not set, leaving the `stop()` cleanup path inconsistent with the eventual `close` event.

## Why This Change Was Made

`unref()` the startup timer so it cannot pin the event loop, and mark the process `closed` on timeout so `stop()` does not try to re-kill an already-terminating child.

## User Impact

The voice-call tunnel startup no longer holds the process open when its caller has moved on; no change to successful tunnel startup.

## Evidence

- Regression test "unrefs the ngrok startup timeout so it cannot keep the host process alive": spies on `setTimeout` and asserts the returned timer's `unref()` is called. **Red before the fix** (`unref` called 0 times), green after.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.test.ts` → 16 passed.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: `startNgrokTunnel` in `extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.ts` started a 30s ngrok-startup timeout with `setTimeout` but never unref'd it, so the host process could be kept alive solely by the pending timer. The fix calls `timeout.unref()` and also marks the tunnel `closed` in the timeout branch before killing the process.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9. The changed timer/unref path is driven through a mocked ngrok child process so the exact `unref()` call is asserted without spawning a real tunnel.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:

Evidence after fix (CI `Real behavior proof` job passed; local suite asserts):
```
- "unrefs the ngrok startup timeout so it cannot keep the host process alive" -> setTimeout's unref() called
```

Observed result after fix: The 30s startup watchdog no longer holds the event loop open, and the timeout branch now marks the tunnel closed before killing the process. The `Real behavior proof` CI check passed for this head.

What was not tested: A real ngrok subprocess and live tunnel was not started (ngrok is fully mocked); the proof targets the exact changed lines — `timeout.unref()` and the `closed` flag in the timeout branch — which are process/timer-control contracts.

target.title: fix(qqbot): cancel non-OK direct-upload response body before throwing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`downloadDirectUploadUrl` in the QQ Bot media module fetches media from direct-upload URLs through `fetchWithSsrFGuard`. When the upstream returns a non-OK response, the code throws immediately without canceling the response body — the unconsumed stream holds a connection open.

## Why This Change Was Made

Follows the same pattern as #109519 (Google Chat), #109508 (docs search), #109701 (MSTeams), #109728 (APNs relay), and #110039 (Telegram media harness) — cancel the response body before throwing so that upstream streams are drained.

## User Impact

No user-facing change. Prevents resource leaks when QQ Bot direct-upload URLs return non-OK HTTP status codes.

## Evidence

### Real HTTP server proof

```
$ node scripts/proofs/qqbot-direct-upload-cancel-proof.mjs
Server: http://127.0.0.1:36215

=== BEFORE (throw without body.cancel) ===
  503 Service Unavailable — body UNCONSUMED

=== AFTER (body?.cancel before throw) ===
  503 Service Unavailable
  body?.cancel() executed ✓
  [server] /direct-upload → client canceled stream ✓

=== PR diff (media.ts:163) ===
  if (!response.ok) {
+   await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined);
    throw new Error(`Failed to download direct upload...`);
```

The proof script starts a real HTTP server returning 503 with a slow binary stream (simulating a QQ Bot direct-upload response), then exercises the exact cancel-before-throw pattern. The server confirms `client canceled stream ✓`.

### Unit test

New test ("cancels a non-OK direct-upload response body before throwing") in `media.test.ts` verifies:
- A real `Response` with status 503 is returned by the fetch mock
- `response.body.cancel()` is called exactly once before the error is thrown
- Token acquisition is NOT attempted after the error

target.title: fix(qa-lab): unref detached qa cli child and detach stdio listeners
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`runQaCli` spawns a **detached** child (non-Windows) but never `unref()`s it and never removes the `stdout`/`stderr` `data` listeners on `close`. On the success path the promise resolves while the detached process and its pipe listeners stay attached, so the parent's event loop cannot exit until the child exits.

## Why This Change Was Made

`unref()` the child after spawn so a completed qa cli run does not keep the caller alive, and remove the data listeners on `close` so the resolved stream is not retained.

## User Impact

QA Lab suite runs and the host process can exit promptly after a qa cli invocation completes; no change to success/failure behavior.

## Evidence

- Regression test "unrefs the detached child so it cannot keep the parent event loop alive": asserts `child.unref()` is called once and stdio `data` listeners are detached on `close`. **Red before the fix** (`unref` called 0 times), green after.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-lab/src/suite-runtime-agent-process.test.ts` → 28 passed.
- Verified `upstream/main` is byte-identical for this region (not yet fixed), so this PR is not a duplicate.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: `runQaCli` in `extensions/qa-lab/src/suite-runtime-agent-process.ts` spawns a detached qa-cli child but never `unref()`s it and never removes the stdout/stderr `data` listeners on close, so the parent's event loop could stay alive (or retain the resolved stream) after the promise settles. The fix calls `child.unref()` and detaches both listeners in the `close` handler.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9. The changed spawn/unref/listener path is driven through a mocked `node:child_process` so the exact `child.unref()` call and listener detachment are asserted without spawning real processes.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run extensions/qa-lab/src/suite-runtime-agent-process.test.ts`

Evidence after fix (CI `Real behavior proof` job passed; local suite asserts):
```
- "unrefs the detached child so it cannot keep the parent event loop alive" -> child.unref called exactly once
- stdout/stderr data listeners removed on close so the resolved stream is not retained
```

Observed result after fix: The detached child is unref'd exactly once and both stream listeners are detached on `close`, so the caller can exit without reaping or retaining the child. The `Real behavior proof` CI check passed for this head.

What was not tested: A real subprocess spawn against a live qa-cli binary was not executed (the spawn is fully mocked); the proof targets the exact changed lines — the `unref()` call and listener cleanup — which are process-control contracts, not business logic.

`currentProviders()` in the session upstream-activity monitor read the **mutable** `getPluginRegistryState()?.activeRegistry` to discover session-catalog providers. This is the same drift class fixed upstream in `session-catalog.ts`, which now reads the bootstrap-pinned `getActivePluginSessionExtensionRegistry()`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Read the pinned session-extension registry (`getActivePluginSessionExtensionRegistry()?.sessionCatalogs`) instead of the mutable `activeRegistry`. The monitor is a persistent loop with no request-scoped pin, so it must use the stable surface the gateway already pins at startup.

## User Impact

The upstream-activity monitor keeps watching the correct session catalogs across plugin-registry churn instead of observing an empty set. No config or protocol change; no migration.

## Evidence

- Regression test `session-upstream-monitor-pinned-registry.test.ts` "reads the pinned session-extension registry after active registry churn": pins a registry carrying the provider, swaps the mutable `activeRegistry` to an empty one, asserts the monitor still calls the pinned provider. **Red before the fix** (`checkUpstreamActivity` called 0 times), green after.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9. The fix is exercised by the existing test suite which drives the real session state database (`openOpenClawStateDatabase`) against throwaway temp dirs and asserts monitor tick behavior end to end.

target.title: fix(ui): bound managed image blob URL fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveManagedOutgoingImageBlobUrl` in `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.ts` fetches a managed chat image blob URL with `fetch(...)` **without any timeout or abort signal**. A stalled image endpoint hangs thumbnail resolution indefinitely.

Same unbounded-network-operation class as the many `fix(...)` "bound X" PRs: a request with no `AbortSignal` can block the caller forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wrap the fetch in an `AbortController` + `setTimeout` watchdog (`MANAGED_IMAGE_BLOB_URL_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000`, alongside the existing `MANAGED_IMAGE_BLOB_URL_MISS_RETRY_MS`), following the Control UI convention. The timer is cleared in `finally`.

## User Impact

Chat image thumbnails fail fast instead of hanging when the image endpoint is slow or down.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.ts` on `main` line 1552: `fetch(fetchUrl, { ... })` has no `signal`.
- Fix threads `controller.signal` into the request and clears the timeout.

Co-Authored-By: opencode <noreply@opencode.ai>
## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: Managed outgoing image blob resolution (`resolveManagedOutgoingImageBlobUrl` in `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.ts`) hangs forever when the gateway image endpoint never responds, because the `fetch(fetchUrl, { ... })` call has no abort signal.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24). The fix applies the same `AbortController` + `setTimeout(..., 30_000)` watchdog threaded into `fetch` as `signal`, cleared in `finally`, that PRs #110009 and #110010 already ship and prove with real local-HTTP-server tests (Nostr profile ops, chat avatar). #110009 / #110010 real-server tests: `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` and `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.test.ts` — both pass, showing a stalled endpoint aborts after the bound and a normal round trip still resolves.

Exact steps or command run after this patch (mode evidence):
- `node /Users/maomaoplanet/Projects/openclaw-evidence/pr-110011/repro.mjs`

Evidence after fix (standalone reproduction of the exact production fetch/signal/watchdog/clearTimeout pattern, using a 1s bound so it runs fast; production uses 30_000ms):
```
STALL  -> rejected: AbortError after 1004ms (bound 1000ms)
NORMAL -> resolved ok=true after 7ms
```

Observed result after fix: A stalled gateway endpoint is aborted via the `AbortController` watchdog (AbortError) instead of leaving the fetch pending forever; a responsive endpoint resolves normally. The production code path is identical to the already-proven #110009 / #110010 pattern, only the fetch target and 30s constant differ.

What was not tested: An in-repo Vitest unit test driving `resolveManagedOutgoingImageBlobUrl` directly was not added because `chat-message.ts` statically imports browser-only components (`@awesome.me/webawesome` tooltips via `copy-button.ts`); the same import chain prevents the pre-existing `chat-message.test.ts` from loading in this environment (and in CI for this checkout), so a direct import test would only add a red job. The pattern itself is proven by the #110009 / #110010 real-server tests plus the standalone reproduction above.

target.title: fix(msteams): bound remote media saves with header and idle timeouts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Microsoft Teams inbound remote media saves could hang indefinitely when an attachment response returned headers and then stalled mid-body. `saveResponseMedia` / `saveRemoteMedia` were called without `readIdleTimeoutMs` (and without a header timeout on the runtime path), so a chunk stall never failed closed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pass the same media timeout policy already used by Mattermost/Zalo/Tlon: `responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000` and `readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000` through both the direct `saveResponseMedia` path and the runtime `saveRemoteMedia` path.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled Teams attachment download body could hang inbound media persistence forever.

**After:** Attachment body reads fail closed after 30s of idle (and header waits after 120s on the guarded path), so the inbound turn can surface a media failure instead of hanging.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.ts`, `extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` → `saveResponseMedia` / `channel.media.saveRemoteMedia`

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

Teams remote media saves now forward header and body-idle timeouts on both media paths.

### Canonical reachability path

`downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` → `saveRemoteMediaDirect` → `saveResponseMedia({ readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`, and the non-direct path → `saveRemoteMedia({ responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000, readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`.

### Real environment tested

Real HTTP transport: a local `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1` that returns `image/png` headers plus one body chunk and then never sends another chunk or ends the response. The production `saveResponseMedia` (from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/media-runtime` — the exact function the direct Teams save path passes `readIdleTimeoutMs` into) is driven against that live socket with a temp `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` media store, Node v22.23.1.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Real HTTP server sends media headers + one chunk then stalls; drive the
# production Teams save path against it (idle budget 300ms):
OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx scripts/proof-msteams-media-idle-timeout.mts

# Supplemental focused regression:
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.test.ts --reporter=dot
```

### Evidence after fix

Real HTTP stall (production Teams save path against a live socket):

```text
  ok: stalled attachment save rejected (not hung) — elapsed=325ms
  ok: save terminated (bounded, not infinite) — elapsed=325ms
  ok: idle-timeout failure surfaced — Failed to fetch media from https://teams.example.com/att.png: Media download stalled: no data received for 300ms
  ok: unbounded attachment read still hanging after 2000ms — state=still-hanging
  ok: completing attachment saved — {}

```

Against a real stalled `image/png` socket, `saveResponseMedia` fails closed in ~325ms with `Media download stalled: no data received for 300ms` and releases the connection. The negative control — an unbounded `arrayBuffer()` on the same socket — is still unresolved after a 2000ms observation window, confirming the pre-fix hang. A well-behaved completing attachment still saves.

### What was not tested

Live stall against a real Microsoft Teams attachment host.

### Fix classification

target.body:
## Summary

- apply portable stdio and remote MCP declarations through OpenClaw's validated source-config writer
- preserve `${ENV_VAR}` references and credential-free OAuth intent without storing server configuration in provenance
- reuse exact existing declarations, distinguish Claw-created from independently owned config, and allow multiple Claws to share one exact server
- expose MCP ownership and drift in status/export and remove only the final unchanged Claw-created declaration

## Contract

- dry-run shows each MCP command or URL before consent; apply rechecks source config and uses create-only writes
- conflicting existing names block add; exact existing declarations are reused without mutation
- provenance stores only agent, name, redacted digest, ownership class, and lifecycle status
- pending writes reconcile deterministically against source config; unreadable source config fails planning before any cleanup
- remove releases independently owned, shared, missing, failed, or operator-modified declarations and uses compare-before-unset for the final Claw-created declaration
- cron jobs are disabled before MCP, agent, package, and workspace cleanup so scheduled work cannot race teardown

target.title: fix(qqbot): resolve start() when abort signal already fired
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stopping the QQBot gateway during or immediately after startup could leave `GatewayConnection.start()` pending forever when the caller AbortSignal was already aborted. The previous lifecycle also continued connecting after an early abort, which could leave a socket created during shutdown outside cleanup ownership.

## Why This Change Was Made

`start()` registered abort listeners after work had already begun without normalizing an already-fired signal. The fix makes abort handling idempotent at registration, skips connection work for pre-aborted starts, and checks lifecycle ownership after each asynchronous startup stage. A socket created after an in-flight abort is closed before it can be adopted. Risk is limited to the QQBot connection startup and shutdown path; no config or protocol surface changes.

## User Impact

QQBot channel stop/restart no longer hangs when shutdown overlaps startup, and startup does not retain a WebSocket that finishes opening after its lifecycle owner has stopped.

## Evidence

**Live configured-account proof (redacted):**

```
credentialExchangeSucceeded: true
abortPhase: after start invocation
outcome: resolved
elapsedMs: 146
existingGatewayLeftRunning: true
```

This ran the exported `GatewayConnection` with the locally configured QQBot app ID and secret file, forced a fresh real QQ credential exchange, then aborted immediately after invoking `start()`. The patched lifecycle resolved in 146 ms after the real credential request and stopped before gateway URL/socket adoption. The already-running live Gateway was left online, and no messages were sent.

**Deterministic before proof on the original implementation:**

```
label: before-fix
timedOut: true
elapsedMs: 501
resolved: false
exit: 1
```

The same exported-class harness with a pre-aborted signal exceeded its 500 ms bound before the fix.

**Focused regression tests:**

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/gateway-connection.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       9 passed (9)
```

Coverage now verifies both that a pre-aborted start performs no socket creation and that a socket returned after an in-flight abort is immediately closed.

**Additional checks:**

```
$ pnpm format extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/gateway-connection.ts extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/gateway-connection.test.ts
Finished on 2 files

$ git diff --check
# clean
```

`pnpm check:changed` attempted to delegate its heavy lane to unavailable maintainer Testbox infrastructure and exited before running the remote check. Full type/lint/build gates are therefore left to GitHub Actions. A full active-service restart was not performed because it would disrupt the existing live channel.

AI-assisted: Codex and Cursor; proof runs executed on this machine.
